discovery: The titanium-sapphire laser and passive mode-locking techniques (Kerr-lens and semiconductor saturable-absorber mode-locking) that created the femtosecond solid-state laser
motivation: Moulton's invention of the titanium-doped sapphire laser (1982) gave physics a broadband, tunable solid-state gain medium. Sibbett's discovery of self-mode-locking (1991), explained as Kerr-lens mode-locking, made sub-10-femtosecond pulses straightforward to produce directly from an oscillator. Keller's semiconductor saturable absorber mirrors (SESAM) made passive mode-locking reliable and self-starting across solid-state, fibre and semiconductor lasers. Together these advances turned femtosecond pulses from an exotic effort into a routine laboratory tool. They form the foundation of chirped-pulse-amplified high-intensity lasers, carrier-envelope-phase-stabilized frequency combs, attosecond science, femtochemistry, multiphoton microscopy and precision industrial and medical laser processing. Few technologies have given us so many new ways to see things no one could see before. This is basic research whose benefits now reach far beyond physics, into biology, medicine and industry.
